implementation_notes: C has no service framework, so sprawl here takes the form of a large number of small binaries or daemons, each with its own process management, config file, logging setup and deployment, communicating over a socket or a pipe. The cost is the same and it is paid in the operating system: a functional decomposition means N process startups, N config schemas and N places for a signal handler to be wrong. C's specific sprawl hazard is that the natural 'service' is a shared library, and promoting a library to a daemon is almost never justified — the only real reasons are an isolation or a scaling boundary, both of which should be named. The detection is the process list in the init system and the count of config files.
idiom_name: one HTTP server or shared library per utility; process-per-function
pitfalls: A daemon per utility turns a library call into a process boundary with all the cost and none of the isolation benefit.
Each daemon with its own config file means an environment change is N edits, which is the cross-cutting change problem at the operating system level.
No typed contract between C services, so a schema change is a coordination problem discovered at runtime rather than at compile time.
